prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Like nights we knelt on the dirt floor of a dugout, leaned our heads back, eyes twitching gone, and popped nitrous canisters into the communion shapes of our mouths, slipped inside where everything seemed to be falling snow, ice, the time split between chasing flies through a darkened park and sprawling in sycamore bark—how clean that abyss we drifted in, like dew, more like pollen, on our skins; and, beneath, a want for touch, a kiss, a return. Like nothing back then, to break an arm latching on to the bumper of an Impala, or settling back as the car took us as far as the salted bridge, before letting the ride go with a mitten caught behind the chrome waving from the other side of the river. Like this, you said, sliding a needle, watching dope plunge, the body's rush and tow until you felt something like an angel hovering above, but it was only pigeon feathers deviling the air. Those friends are gone: some dead, dying, locked up or jailed in themselves; and when I see some kids running in the heat of a taillight swirling behind them, I remember we wanted only to quiet our bodies, their unnatural hum, a vague pull inward, some thin furrows gliding over the snow.

outputs.L2:
Some evenings found us crouched on the packed earth of a dugout's floor, tilting our faces skyward as our eyes flickered and rolled back, cracking open nitrous canisters against our open mouths like some strange sacrament. We'd disappear into a world that felt entirely composed of falling snow and ice, our attention divided between stalking flies across a shadowed playground and collapsing against the rough skin of sycamore trees. That emptiness we floated through felt so pure—settling on our flesh like morning dew, or perhaps more like drifting pollen—yet underneath it all lingered a hunger for contact, for a kiss, for something to come back to.

Nothing seemed reckless then—not even snapping an arm while gripping the rear bumper of a passing Impala, letting the vehicle drag us onward until we reached the ice-crusted bridge, finally releasing our hold as a mitten snagged on the chrome trim, fluttering back at us from across the water like a farewell.

This is how it's done, you told me once, guiding the needle in, the two of us watching the drug disappear into the vein, feeling that surge and undertow move through our bodies until something resembling an angel seemed to hover close by—though really it was nothing more than pigeon feathers stirring restlessly through the air.

Most of those companions have scattered now—some buried, some fading, others confined behind bars or trapped within the walls of their own minds. Watching children dash through the heated shimmer trailing behind a car's taillights brings it all back: how we'd only ever wanted to still our restless bodies, to silence that strange internal buzzing, that faint pull drawing us inward, like the shallow tracks left behind in snow.
outputs.L3:
# Nights in the Dugout

The nights blur together now, but the ritual never changed: kneeling on packed dirt floors, the cold seeping through denim at the knees, hands trembling slightly as we cracked open canister after canister of nitrous oxide. The hiss of gas, the balloon filling, the inhale—and then the world would dissolve into something like snowfall. Not real snow, but a numbing white oblivion that blanketed everything sharp and painful about being young and lost. For those few seconds, nothing existed except the rushing static in our skulls, a temporary erasure of whatever it was we were all running from.

But beneath that manufactured emptiness, something else lived—something the drugs could dull but never quite kill. It was a hunger for human touch, for the kind of connection that made you feel real, tethered to another person instead of floating alone in your own head. We were all searching for belonging in the wrong places, mistaking chemical closeness for the genuine article, chasing a high that promised warmth but delivered only isolation dressed up as togetherness.

That same reckless hunger for feeling *something* bled into everything else we did. I remember gripping the bumper of a moving car, crouched low, wind tearing at my clothes, my knuckles white against the metal—letting go only when the bridge loomed ahead, close enough that survival wasn't guaranteed. There was no calculation in it, no weighing of risk. Just the raw, stupid fearlessness of youth, the sense that death was an abstraction that happened to other people, not to us.

Heroin brought its own hallucinations, its own cruel poetry. I remember believing I saw angels once, wings unfurling in some corner of my vision, a moment of transcendence that felt holy. Only later did I understand it was nothing—just pigeon feathers scattered on pavement, caught in a trick of light and a mind desperate to find meaning in the mundane. The drug didn't grant visions; it just lowered the threshold for what we were willing to believe.

So many of the people who knelt beside me in that dugout, who let go of that bumper, who chased those same false angels—they're gone now in one way or another. Some are dead. Some are locked away behind bars, their reckless years finally catching up with consequence. Others are alive but imprisoned differently, trapped inside themselves, unable to escape the very restlessness we all once tried to numb into silence.

Now, when I watch children playing—innocent, unburdened, still years away from whatever hunger might eventually gnaw at them—I think of all of us back then. We were just kids too, aching for something we couldn't name, trying anything to quiet a noise inside us that never seemed to stop. I wonder if they'll find a way to quiet theirs before it costs them what it cost us.
outputs.L4:
**Static and Flight**

I remember the hiss of the canister, that cold rush filling my lungs like liquid silver, the world tilting sideways into brightness before folding back on itself. We did it in parking lots, in basements, in the backseats of cars that weren't ours—chasing that half-second of nothing, that pure white static where the self dissolved and there was only the falling, the floating, the blessed absence of everything that hurt.

We skitched, too—crouched low behind bumpers, gloved hands gripping cold metal, sneakers sliding on wet asphalt as the car dragged us into speed we hadn't earned. The wind tore at our faces. Someone always screamed, half terror, half joy. It didn't matter if we lived. That was the point, maybe—the not mattering. The body became a thing we could leave, if only for the length of a city block, a held breath, a held nerve.

Later there were needles. The metal in the skin was almost tender, an intimacy stranger than any touch—the way the body opened for the escape, welcomed it, begged for it. We were seventeen and starving for the sensation of disappearing. We called it living because we didn't have another word for wanting to be gone.

I think of them now—the friends who rode beside me into all that stupid brilliance. Danny is dead, has been for years, found alone in a room that still smelled like him. Marcus is in a cell somewhere upstate, writing letters that arrive smudged and late. Sara is alive but not present—she moves through days like a ghost wearing her own name, trapped behind eyes that used to laugh so easily. Of all of us, I don't know who escaped and who was simply spared a little longer.

We told ourselves we were chasing highs, chasing speed, chasing the electric thrill of almost-dying. But looking back, I think we were only trying to find quiet. Underneath all that velocity was a stillness we couldn't reach any other way—a held breath, a suspended second, the closest thing to peace our restless, aching bodies could find. We wanted, more than anything, to stop—not to die, but to rest, to be still inside our own skins for once.

It wasn't nihilism. It wasn't even really about oblivion, not at its core. It was about connection—to sensation, to each other, to something larger than the constant hum of wanting that lived beneath our ribs. We held onto car bumpers and each other's hands with the same desperate grip, searching for a way out of ourselves that might, somehow, lead us back in.

Now there is only this: memory, and the terrible tenderness of counting who's left. The rush is gone, replaced by something slower, sadder, more honest. I sit with what remains—the ache, the quiet, the names of the ones I loved who couldn't find their way to stillness except through leaving entirely. And I understand, finally, that we were never reckless. We were only searching, in the only language we knew, for a way to be at peace inside our own restless hearts.
outputs.L5:
# The Impala's Grace

There's something remarkable about watching a herd of impala move across the savanna. Those slender antelopes, with their reddish-brown coats and curved horns, seem to defy gravity when they leap. Like dancers choreographed by instinct alone, they bound through tall grass in perfect synchronization, covering distances of up to ten meters in a single jump.

Those who have witnessed this spectacle in person often describe it as mesmerizing. The impala's ability to change direction mid-air, almost like a feint in sports, confuses predators just long enough to escape. This evasive technique, called "stotting" or "pronking," isn't just about speed—it's a display of vigor that tells lions and cheetahs: catching me would be too costly an effort.

Social behavior among these animals is equally fascinating. Male impalas establish territories during mating season, and those who succeed in defending their ground gather harems of females. The clashing of horns during these confrontations sounds like distant thunder rolling across the plains, a reminder of nature's persistent rhythms of competition and survival.

What makes the impala so compelling isn't just its physical beauty, but the way it embodies balance—between vulnerability and resilience, between individual instinct and collective safety in numbers. Those who study African wildlife often point to the impala as a perfect example of evolutionary elegance, a creature perfectly adapted to its environment.

In many ways, watching an impala navigate its world is like observing nature's own poetry in motion—swift, precise, and endlessly graceful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about reckless teenage years, drug use, and lost friendships, using vivid winter imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Frostbite**

We were matches struck against December,
flaring gold in parking lots behind the school,
our breath ghosting up like something holy
though there was nothing holy in us then.

Sixteen and starving for something
we couldn't name, we filled our pockets
with pills bright as candy, with baggies
that crinkled like frozen leaves,
and called it living.

Marcus taught me how to hold smoke
in my lungs the way you hold a secret—
too long, until it hurts, until it becomes
part of your blood. That winter
his eyes went the color of iced-over ponds,
something moving beneath the surface
that I couldn't reach.

We drove too fast down black-ice roads,
windows cracked despite the cold,
music screaming louder than the wind,
convinced we were immortal,
convinced the frost creeping up the glass
was decoration and not warning.

I remember Sarah's laugh before it changed,
before her pupils became small dark stones
sunk in snow, before she stopped
answering when I said her name
like it used to mean something.

We were a bonfire in a blizzard—
brilliant, doomed, throwing sparks
that melted small circles in the white
before the cold took back what was hers.

Some nights I still feel that particular chill,
the one that isn't weather
but is the space where people used to be—
Marcus in Colorado, unrecognizable now,
Sarah just a name I don't say out loud,
the rest of us scattered like frost patterns
that seemed permanent on the window
until the sun came up
and there was only glass,
clear and empty,
showing the plain gray no confidences no world 
we'd traded everything to avoid.

I am older now. I flinch
at the smell of certain smoke.
I still hear the ice cracking
underneath us all those years,
how we danced on it anyway,
how some of us
are still underwater,

how winter always ends
but doesn't always
let you leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nostalgic, gritty poem in the style of confessional poetry about youth, addiction, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Needle Remembers**

I was seventeen the summer the copper pipes
sang under Third Street, and Denny's parking lot
smelled like rain on hot tar and cigarette punk—
we thought we were forever then,
passing the bottle like a sacrament
we didn't know we'd worship into ruin.

Mama's rosary is still in the glovebox
of a car I sold for gas money and shame.
I used to pray with different hands.
Now I pray with the practiced twitch
of someone counting days like rosary beads—
thirty-one, thirty-two, don't look back
at the boy who thought Bobby's laugh
would outlive the overdose,
thought Jenny's hair would always smell
like drugstore vanilla and want.

They don't tell you grief has a taste—
metallic, like biting foil,
like the year you turned twenty
and buried three friends
before you'd paid off your first car.

I used to think the body was a temple.
Now I know it's more like a house fire—
you keep running back in
for what you think you can't live without,
and mostly you're wrong,
and mostly you go back anyway.

Somewhere in Ohio there's a photograph
of five kids on a hood, all teeth and cheap beer,
none of us knowing yet
which one the years would take first,
which one would get clean
and spend the rest of his life
apologizing to mirrors.

I am the one who lived.
I say this without triumph—
say it like a man counting scars,
say it like a name I'm still learning
to answer to.

Some nights I still hear the highway
the way it sounded at 3 a.m., windows down,
Bobby singing off-key, Jenny laughing
like she owned the dark—
and I let myself believe, just for a second,
that death is a rumor,
that the road goes on forever,

that we are still those reckless gods
who thought the needle was a kind of prayer,
who thought the burning
was the same as being alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long single-sentence poem structured with repeated "Like..." clauses recalling dangerous childhood memories.
counterfactuals.output:
**What We Didn't Know Could Kill Us**

Like the way we rode our bikes no-handed down Miller's Hill where the road forgot to have a stop sign at the bottom, arms out like we were already flying before we knew what falling cost, and like the creek behind the Hendersons' where we dared each other across the rusted pipe, six feet above the water, arms windmilling, laughing like the drop wasn't real, like the ice on Miller's Pond in February that groaned under our boots but held, held, held until it didn't for Tommy Alvarez who came up soaked and blue-lipped and we dragged him home and never told, like the fireworks we lit in Dylan's backyard with our bare hands too close, the way sparks kissed our knuckles and we called it nothing, called it fine, like the time we climbed the water tower because someone said we couldn't, the rust flaking under our palms, the town spread out below us small as a memory we hadn't made yet, like the train tracks we walked balance-beam style, ears tuned for a whistle that always came later than we expected, like the matches we struck in the tool shed just to watch the flame eat air, just to feel our hearts go quick and bright as the fire itself, like the dogs we didn't know were dangerous, the fences we didn't know were electric, the pills in grandma's cabinet we didn't know were sleep, like the boy who dared us into the abandoned house on Curtis Street where the floor groaned like something waking, like the lake at midnight, clothes flung on the dock, water black and bottomless and cold enough to stop a heart, like the fistfights that ended in blood and laughter both, like the hands we let hold ours too tight, too early, too much like something we hadn't yet been taught to name, like every single ordinary Tuesday we walked home alone past dark yards and darker cars, invincible in the particular way that only children are, believing danger was a story that happened to someone else, some other kid in some other town, until we grew up enough to look back and count — quietly, alone, in rooms far from all of it — how many almosts it took to make an after, how many small gods must have been watching, how much of it was luck dressed up as childhood, how close we came, again and again, to never getting to remember any of this at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem about growing up rough in a working-class town, referencing drugs, cars, and friends who didn't make it.
counterfactuals.output:
# Concrete Roots

Cracked sidewalks raised us, not some picket fence,
Where the mill's last breath still hung like incense
Over row houses leaning into each other's shoulders,
Watching us grow up faster, watching us grow older

Before our time, before we had the choice—
Chevy engines were the only voice
That made sense in a town the world forgot,
Revving loud through streets where hope was shot

Ricky sold what Tommy learned to need,
Both of them just chasing something, planting seed
In soil too poisoned for a harvest clean,
I watched them fade like smoke, like it was routine

We'd pile four deep in a beat-up car,
Windows down, radio playing loud, not far
From anywhere that mattered, just driving
Through the only world we knew, surviving

Danny didn't make it past nineteen,
Found him where the railroad tracks convene
With Third and Oak—they said it was the pills,
Said a lot of things about our splintered hills

But we kept driving, kept the engine running,
Some kind of faith in forward motion, cunning
Enough to know that stillness was the death
Of something in us, some collective breath

Now I drive these streets and count the ghosts,
The empty lots, the ones who loved me most
Who didn't make the drive to see the other side—
This town still runs on love and loss, still runs on pride

We were rough-cut diamonds no one came to find,
Grown up rough, but growing all the same, combined
By struggle into something like a family—
Even now, that town still runs in me
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, image-heavy poem exploring the fine line between danger and beauty in adolescence, ending with a reflection on loss.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Fire Remembers

At fifteen, we were matchsticks
striking ourselves against anything—
curb, boy, bottle, dare—
just to watch what colors
we could become.

The girls I loved wore danger
like cheap perfume, too much,
applied in gas station bathrooms
with shaking hands and stolen
tubes of lipstick the shade
of warning signs.

We drove too fast down backroads
that dissolved into cornfields,
windows open, screaming songs
we didn't understand yet,
believing the wind could carry
whatever we were becoming
somewhere safer than ourselves.

There was a boy who taught me
how a bruise could bloom
like something beautiful—
purple-yellow constellation
mapping where his hands had been,
and I wore it like a medal,
like proof I'd survived
something worth surviving.

We smoked in parking lots
at 2 a.m., ash falling
like grey snow onto shoulders
that hadn't learned yet
they were breakable,
thinking the cherry-glow
of cigarettes was the same
as being seen, being warm,
being wanted.

Everything was a threshold then—
every party a door
we walked through sideways,
every empty house a church
where we practiced our own
undoing, learning the liturgy
of almost, of nearly,
of *just this once*.

The beauty was the danger.
The danger was the only thing
that felt like being alive—
electric, humming, close
to something that could burn us
or baptize us,
we couldn't always tell
which, and didn't care.

Now I'm older, and I miss it
the way you'd miss a house
that caught fire while you slept—
grief for something
that could have killed you,
that maybe should have,
and didn't, and left you
standing in the ash
of who you might have been,

wondering what it means
to survive your own becoming,
to look back at the girl
who lit herself up
just to see if she would burn,

and find you cannot save her,
cannot warn her,
can only watch her
disappear like smoke—
gorgeous, and gone,
and never coming back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
